transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I suppose I'm here because... well, it's about my work. I'm a translator and interpreter, mostly dealing with highly technical documents, legal contracts, things where precision isn't just preferred, it's absolutely critical. And for months now, I've been noticing this... this pattern in the project files. It started small, almost imperceptible, really. Just tiny, microscopic changes to the translation memory database. A word swapped here, a phrase slightly altered there, always in sections I had already finalized and signed off on. 

At first, I thought, okay, maybe it's a glitch, or maybe I'm just tired. But then the timestamps started shifting. I'd finish a file at, say, 4:15 PM, and the system would suddenly show it was modified at 4:18 PM, right after I logged out. And it's not random. It's very specific. It's certain subcontractors we use, and there's this one colleague in particular—I won't name him yet, but he's always the one assigned to the final review stage right after me. 

They are deliberately going in and making these minuscule errors, adjusting the timestamps, and basically doctoring the files so it looks like my quality control failed. Like I'm the one making the mistakes. I even went to IT about it. I sat down with the lead technician, showed him the discrepancies, the timeline, everything. And he looked at the audit trail and had the nerve to tell me it was clean. He said the logs showed no unauthorized access. But of course they wouldn't, would they? If you're going to go to the trouble of sabotaging someone's work, you're going to make sure the record is arranged to cover your tracks and put the blame squarely on me. It's incredibly frustrating, and honestly, it's starting to affect my ability to just sit down and do my job, because I know they're just waiting to alter my next submission.
Have you ever heard voices, sounds, or whispering when there is no one around?

Voices? No, no, nothing like that. I mean, my hearing is perfectly fine, probably better than average given how much time I spend listening to nuances in language and tone during consecutive interpretation sessions. But no, I don't hear whispering or phantom sounds or anything of the sort. I'm completely grounded in reality, Doctor. That's actually the entire point, isn't it? I am paying attention to what is actually happening right in front of me, on my screen, in the server logs. 

If anything, it's the silence that's deafening. The complete lack of accountability. When I'm sitting in my home office, it's just the hum of the computer and the sound of my own typing. It's very quiet. And that quiet just gives me more time to think about how meticulously they are orchestrating this. You don't need to hear voices to know when you're being undermined. The evidence is all there, silently sitting in the metadata, waiting for someone to actually look at it without an agenda. I don't need hallucinations to tell me my work is being tampered with; the altered timestamps and the sudden, inexplicable typos in my finalized drafts do all the talking.
Have you been diagnosed with any medical conditions, or noticed any recent changes in your physical health?

Medical conditions? No, I mean, I don't have any major medical issues. I've always been pretty healthy, honestly. I try to take care of myself. I make sure I get up and walk around during the day, you know, because sitting at a desk doing translation work for eight, ten, sometimes twelve hours a day can really take a toll on your back and your circulation if you're not careful. I use a standing desk for part of the day, and I'm very particular about my ergonomic setup—the chair height, the monitor distance, all of that. It's essential when your livelihood depends on being at a computer. 

But as for actual medical diagnoses, no. My blood pressure is fine, my cholesterol is normal, at least it was at my last physical about... oh, it must have been eight or nine months ago. The doctor said everything looked perfectly standard for a man my age. I haven't noticed any sudden changes, either. No unexplained weight loss or gain, no weird pains, nothing like that. I do get a little eye strain sometimes, but that's just an occupational hazard, isn't it? Staring at dual monitors, comparing source texts with target texts, scrutinizing every single character... it tires the eyes out. But I have blue-light blocking glasses for that, and I use artificial tears if they get dry. 

Honestly, the only thing that's been affecting me physically lately is the stress of this whole situation at work. It's the tension. You know when you're just constantly on edge, waiting for the other shoe to drop? I carry it in my shoulders. I'll be sitting there, reviewing a document I *know* I already perfected, and I'll find another one of those deliberate little errors they slipped in, and my jaw just clenches. I've been grinding my teeth a bit at night, I think. I wake up and my jaw feels tight. And my sleep hasn't been great, but that's not a medical condition, that's just the natural physical response to being targeted and gaslit by your own colleagues and IT department. Anyone would feel physically drained if they had to spend half their day doing their job and the other half trying to meticulously document how they are being sabotaged. But no, no actual medical conditions or diseases or anything like that. Just the physical toll of having to constantly watch my back.
Outside of this situation at work, have you often felt throughout your life that friends, family, or partners were untrustworthy or working against you?

No, no, not at all. Actually, it's quite the opposite. I’ve always prided myself on having very solid, very transparent relationships. My wife, for instance—we’ve been married for fourteen years, we actually met back when I was finishing my master's degree. She’s an archivist, so she understands the value of preserving the exact integrity of a document just as much as I do, maybe even more so. We have a wonderful marriage, built on absolute trust. I’ve never once doubted her, or felt like she was working against me or hiding anything. 

And my family... well, my parents passed a few years ago, but my younger brother and I are very close. He’s an actuary over in Boston, and we talk on the phone every Sunday evening without fail. There’s no drama, no hidden agendas, no feeling that he's untrustworthy. 

Even with friends, you know, I keep a relatively small circle. It's mostly people I’ve known since my early days doing freelance localization, but they are incredibly supportive. We refer clients to each other, we bounce difficult translation phrasing off each other when we get stuck on a tricky colloquialism. I've never felt like any of them were trying to undermine me or steal my clients. 

That’s really why this whole situation with the agency is so completely jarring to me. I am not, by nature, a suspicious person. I don’t go through life looking over my shoulder, I don't think my neighbors are spying on me, I don't think the barista at the coffee shop is out to get me. I expect professionals to act like professionals. 

Honestly, I think that’s exactly why this specific colleague and those subcontractors thought they could get away with it for so long. They probably looked at me and saw someone who is straightforward, someone who trusts the system, and they figured I wouldn't bother to dig into the backend timestamps or scrutinize the translation memory logs once a project was flagged as complete. They took my natural trust in people and tried to weaponize it against me, assuming I'd just accept the errors as my own. So, to answer your question, no. Outside of this very specific, very documented issue at work, my relationships are completely fine. It’s just this one localized environment where the sabotage is happening, and it's strictly professional.
